items.answer: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
Latency is the time delay, or time gap, in virtual reality between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.
Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

questions.question: What is the intended experience of the Majuli virtual reality tour?
options: an immersive interactive medical training experience
an immersive interactive gaming entertainment experience
an immersive interactive heritage experience
an immersive interactive automobile showcase experience
questions.explanation: The Majuli tour is meant to let visitors interactively experience the island's ecological and cultural heritage. The other options name other VR application domains, not the purpose of this case study.

questions.question: Why does the Majuli tour mix walking with teleportation or a vehicle metaphor?
options: the multimodal archive's size can make a single navigation technique weak
the regular system limits can make a single navigation technique weak
video playback needs can make a single navigation technique weak
the island's geographical spread can make a single navigation technique weak
questions.explanation: Because the island is geographically spread, walking alone or teleportation alone may not suit the whole tour, so different navigation techniques are combined. The other factors affect rendering or storage, not the choice of navigation metaphor.

questions.question: What creates the two levels of extensive content in the Majuli tour?
options: many information points that each hold many points of interest
many 3D models that each hold many points of interest
many images that each hold many points of interest
many videos that each hold many points of interest
questions.explanation: The first level is the set of geographically spread information points, and the second level is the many points of interest inside each information point. Multimedia items such as images, videos, or 3D models do not form that two-level structure.

questions.question: What makes rendering the Majuli application more demanding than rendering a simple static image?
options: teleportation between points that can be interactively changed
rich multimodal content that can be interactively changed
geographical spread of points that can be interactively changed
regular images and text that can be interactively changed
questions.explanation: The application's high rendering cost comes from rich multimodal content, including interactively changed videos and animations, which regular systems cannot support without optimization. Navigation layout or basic images and text do not by themselves create that level of computational demand.

data.text: The Majuli VR case study is an immersive, interactive tour of a large river island's ecological and cultural heritage. Its content is extensive because it has many spread-out information points, each with many points of interest and several media types. The island's scale also leads to mixed navigation, with walking inside places and teleportation or vehicle metaphors between places. Because the resulting application is large and its interactive rendering is computationally demanding, regular systems cannot support it, so resource optimization is needed.
points: Majuli is the world's largest inhabited river island, in eastern India on the Brahmaputra.
The Majuli VR tour immerses visitors in interactive exploration of the island's ecological and cultural heritage.
The Majuli tour's two-level content has many spread-out information points, each with many points of interest and multimodal media.
The tour uses walking inside information points and teleportation or vehicle metaphors between them, as the island is large.
Regular systems cannot support the near-10 GB Majuli VR app, so resource optimization supports fast storage and computation.

questions.question: Why did the application deployed on the Oculus Quest 2 need resource optimization?
options: The device has less compute and storage than a high-end workstation
The device has no processor or memory of its own
The device has to be tethered to a fixed high-end workstation
The device has more compute and storage than a high-end workstation
questions.explanation: The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone device with its own processor and memory, but it has less computing power and relatively less storage than a high-end workstation, so the application had to be optimized.

questions.question: How did the Oculus Quest 2 application obtain a selected video?
options: by loading it from the cloud
by retrieving it from a tethered computer
by reading it from local storage
by copying it from the handheld controllers
questions.explanation: Selected video content in the Oculus Quest 2 application is loaded from cloud storage instead of being kept on the headset.

questions.question: What new requirement did remote video storage introduce for the Oculus Quest 2 deployment?
options: steady tethered computer support
large local storage support
real-time network support
extra handheld controller support
questions.explanation: Because the videos were loaded from a remote server, the deployment depended on sufficient network support, including high bandwidth, coverage, and low latency.

questions.question: What effect did storing videos in the cloud have on the Oculus Quest 2 client deployment?
options: It removed the need for any network support
It increased the need for local video storage
It reduced local size and associated computation
It made the headset depend on a tethered computer
questions.explanation: Moving video content to the cloud reduced application size and computation on the Oculus Quest 2 client.

data.text: The Oculus Quest 2 application had to be optimized because the standalone headset has less computing power and storage than a high-end workstation. Storing videos in the cloud and loading them when selected reduced local storage, data access, app size, and computation. This cloud-based benefit depends on a network with sufficient bandwidth, coverage, and low latency to load high-quality videos in real time.
points: The standalone Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and storage than high-end workstations, needing size and computation reduction.
The Quest 2 app stored all videos, not images, in the cloud and loaded selected videos on demand.
Cloud video loading reduced the Oculus Quest 2 app to 5.1 GB and reduced its computation.
Cloud video loading on Quest 2 needed high bandwidth, network coverage, and minimal latency for real-time high-quality video loading.

questions.question: Why did the Majuli virtual tour require an optimization strategy for deployment on a smartphone in a cardboard headset?
options: Because the island's large geographical spread typically made walking alone unsuitable for the tour
Because the full system's size and computation exceed what average smartphones typically support
Because average smartphones typically struggle to display stereoscopic views without an expensive headset
Because a cardboard headset typically struggles to show stereoscopic views without an expensive headset
questions.explanation: The full Majuli system was too large and computationally demanding for typical smartphones, so a reduced deployment strategy was needed. The cardboard headset itself can work with a smartphone displaying stereoscopic views.

questions.question: Which changes made the Majuli virtual tour suitable for a low-cost smartphone and cardboard deployment?
options: Compressing the images and removing video playback support
Compressing the videos and keeping the images unchanged
Reducing the information points and removing walking navigation
Replacing 360-degree images with drone shots of the landscape
questions.explanation: The smartphone/cardboard version reduced storage by compressing images and dropped video playback because most videos could not be used in that deployment. Other changes were not the stated optimization strategy.

questions.question: Why might a developer consider cloud-based services when optimizing a VR experience for a constrained device?
options: Because they could make image compression unnecessary
Because they could allow video playback to be retained
Because they could replace the smartphone's display with a standalone panel
Because they could remove the need for network coverage
questions.explanation: Cloud-based services can let video playback remain while keeping local resources down, but they still depend on network conditions and do not generally replace image compression.

data.text: Adapting the Majuli VR case study to cheap smartphone-based cardboard VR requires reducing its demands. Because an average smartphone cannot support the full system's size and computation, images were compressed and video playback was removed, making the experience less realistic but much smaller. More generally, resource-constrained platforms may require compression, cloud services, or feature removal when a device cannot render a full immersive experience.
points: A cardboard virtual reality headset places a smartphone in a housing to give immersive stereoscopic views cheaply.
Deploying Majuli VR on a smartphone/cardboard needed optimization because its full size and computation exceeded average smartphones.
Removing video playback and compressing images made Majuli VR less realistic, shrinking it from roughly 10 GB to 0.7 GB.
Full immersive VR systems cannot run on platforms that cannot render them; compression, cloud, or feature removal may help.

questions.question: In the NPTEL computer graphics MOOC, what can be studied in more detail?
options: the stages of interactive system requirement gathering
the stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline
the stages of VR resource optimization
the stages of virtual reality system development
questions.explanation: The NPTEL computer graphics MOOC is indicated for detailed study of the stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline. The other stage lists are not the detailed topic identified for that MOOC.

questions.question: What role does the Oxford University Press book Computer Graphics serve for a learner of the computer graphics topics?
options: the source for the topics and a route to interactive system design
the source for the topics and a route to more detailed study
the source for the topics and a route to NPTEL course content
the source for the topics and a route to VR hardware comparison
questions.explanation: The Oxford University Press book Computer Graphics is the source from which the topics were taken and can be used for more detailed study. It is not described as a route to NPTEL content, VR hardware comparison, or interactive system design.

data.text: VR resource optimization topics can be studied further through computer graphics resources. The Oxford University Press book Computer Graphics is the source for those topics. The NPTEL MOOC on computer graphics can also teach those topics and the three-dimensional graphics pipeline stages.
points: The Oxford University Press book Computer Graphics is the source for VR resource optimization topics, giving more detail.
The NPTEL MOOC on computer graphics can teach VR resource optimization topics and three-dimensional graphics pipeline stages.

questions.question: Why can storing videos in the cloud reduce the storage and computation needed for the Majuli virtual tour on an Oculus Quest 2?
questions.reference_answer: Cloud-based video loading keeps videos, which take more space than images, out of the local application. A user can select a video thumbnail and load the chosen video from the cloud instead of storing it on the Oculus Quest 2. This reduces storage and data-access requirements, and because reducing size reduces rendering requirements and memory access, the client application was reduced to 5.1GB, with a corresponding computational reduction.

questions.question: How do image compression and removal of video playback address the storage problem for the smartphone/cardboard deployment of the Majuli virtual reality system?
questions.reference_answer: Deploying the full Majuli virtual reality system on a smartphone in a cardboard required optimization because its size and computation exceed what average smartphones typically support. Compressing images reduces the storage requirement, and removing video playback, since most videos could not be utilized, helps reduce the overall size. Together, compressing the images and removing video playback support reduced the overall size from about 10GB to 0.7GB.

questions.question: Why does the Majuli virtual tour use walking within each information point but teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between information points?
questions.reference_answer: The Majuli tour contains many geographically spread information points, each with many points of interest. Walking is used within each information point, while teleportation or a vehicle metaphor is used between points, because a single technique alone may not suit the island's large geographical spread.
